paragraphs: Izu Peninsula, 90 minutes from Tokyo by Shinkansen to Atami or Mishima. A volcanic peninsula with hot springs, dramatic coastline, and fewer tourists per kilometer than anywhere in the Hakone area. Shuzenji in the central valley is a small onsen town with a classic feel — a bamboo grove along the river, wooden onsen hotels, a 9th-century Buddhist temple. Enough for a full day without a crowd problem.

sections.heading: Mashiko
paragraphs: Mashiko, two hours from Ueno by train (JR Utsunomiya plus bus). A ceramics town that became famous when the potter Shoji Hamada established a studio there in the 1920s and invited other ceramicists. There are now around 300 kilns in and around the town. The spring and autumn pottery fairs are among the best craft markets in Japan. The Hamada Shoji Memorial Mashiko Sankokan museum is on the original estate and worth two hours. The journey requires planning but the experience is unique.

title: Omiyage: The Art of Bringing Back the Right Thing
excerpt: Returning from anywhere in Japan without gifts for the people you left behind is not a neutral act. Omiyage culture runs deep, and buying well requires knowing the rules.
heroImageAlt: Beautifully packaged Japanese confectionery boxes displayed at a station gift shop
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: What omiyage is
paragraphs: Omiyage — travel souvenirs intended for others — is a structured practice in Japan, not an afterthought. When Japanese people return from a trip, they bring back regional food gifts for coworkers, family, and neighbors. The obligation is real enough that Japanese airports, train stations, and tourist areas are built around it: the gift shops at major stations are not concessions but primary retail destinations designed for the specific purpose of providing appropriately packaged regional food at prices calibrated for group gifting.

sections.heading: What makes good omiyage
paragraphs: What constitutes good omiyage. The best gifts are things that are genuinely regional — a sweet or confection from a specific prefecture that can't be bought in Tokyo or wherever you're returning to. Kyoto's Yatsuhashi (cinnamon-flavored triangular confections, raw or baked, in a range of fillings), Hiroshima's Momiji Manju (maple-leaf-shaped cakes with red bean or cream filling), Sapporo's Royce chocolate — these are the canonical examples, and they work because they represent a place specifically. Generic Japan gifts (things with sakura or Mt. Fuji printed on them) are less appreciated.

sections.heading: Format matters
paragraphs: Format matters. Omiyage is given in individually portioned packages, usually 6, 10, or 15 pieces, because it will be shared across a group. A single item that can't be divided is not omiyage. The packaging is typically beautiful and part of the gift — Japanese confectionery packaging has been developed over centuries into a minor art form.

sections.heading: What to bring home
paragraphs: For the visitor bringing things home to other countries: apply the same logic. Regional Japanese sweets in their original packaging travel well, communicate where you've been specifically, and arrive looking intentional. Matcha Kit Kats and regional chip flavors are the casual version. For something more considered: Hikari Kinako (roasted soybean flour snacks from Kyoto), wagashi (traditional confections) from an established Kyoto confectioner like Toraya, or a small tin of gyokuro tea from Uji.

sections.heading: Where to buy
paragraphs: Where to buy: the station gift shops (ekimachibu) in major Shinkansen stations have the best regional selection for your exact route. Kyoto Station has an excellent floor of Kyoto-specific gifts. Tokyo Station's basement has confections from across Japan, which is useful if you forgot to buy in-region but want regional gifts. Department stores have the most curated selection at the highest price; convenience store gift sections exist but should be a last resort.

title: The Hidden Shrines of Kyoto Locals Still Keep Secret
excerpt: Beyond Fushimi Inari and Kinkaku-ji lies another Kyoto — quiet, moss-covered, and entirely yours. We asked local monks and longtime residents where they actually go when the crowds become too much. These are the shrines that rarely appear in guidebooks.
heroImageAlt: A quiet moss-covered shrine path in Kyoto lined with stone lanterns
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Why the famous shrines feel the way they do
paragraphs: Fushimi Inari and Kinkaku-ji are famous because they are genuinely extraordinary, and the crowds are the price of that. But they set an expectation that Kyoto is a place you queue for. It isn't. Kyoto has well over a thousand shrines and temples, and the overwhelming majority of them see almost nobody on a weekday morning. The difference between the Kyoto of the guidebooks and the Kyoto people live in is roughly a fifteen-minute walk in any direction.

sections.heading: Nonomiya, and the walk that gets you there
paragraphs: Nonomiya-jinja sits inside the Arashiyama bamboo grove, which sounds like the opposite of a hidden shrine. The trick is timing and direction. The grove is packed from mid-morning; before eight it is nearly silent. Nonomiya itself is small, mossy, and built around a torii made of unstripped oak with the bark still on it — an unusually old style. Historically it was where imperial princesses purified themselves before being sent to serve at Ise. It takes ten minutes to visit and rewards standing still.

sections.heading: Kurama and Kibune, for the half-day version
paragraphs: North of the city, the Eizan line runs up into the mountains to Kurama. The shrine complex climbs the hillside in stages, and a hiking trail continues over the ridge and down to Kibune on the other side — roughly an hour of walking through cedar roots and stone steps. Kibune-jinja at the far end is approached by a stone staircase lined with red lanterns, which is one of the more photographed stairways in Japan and still, somehow, usually quiet. Do it in that direction: uphill first, downhill into dinner.

sections.heading: The neighbourhood shrines nobody lists
paragraphs: The real find is the category rather than the specific address. Almost every Kyoto neighbourhood has a small shrine wedged between houses, with a torii barely wider than a doorway, a hand-washing basin, and a resident cat. These have no English signage, no entry fee, and no listing anywhere. Walk the residential streets of Nishijin, or the blocks behind the Kamo river north of Demachiyanagi, and you will pass several. They are not secrets so much as things nobody thought to advertise.

sections.heading: How to behave when you are the only one there
paragraphs: An empty shrine asks more of you than a busy one, because there is no crowd to copy. The sequence is short: bow once at the torii, keep to the side of the path rather than the centre, rinse your left hand then your right at the basin, and if you approach the hall, the standard form is two bows, two claps, a pause, one bow. A coin in the box is customary and any amount is fine. Nobody is grading you, and getting the order slightly wrong is not an offence.

sections.heading: A note on what 'hidden' should mean
paragraphs: There is an obvious tension in publishing a list of quiet places. The shrines above absorb visitors well because they are spread out and because most of them are still functioning neighbourhood institutions rather than attractions. The way to keep them that way is unglamorous: go early, keep your voice down, don't photograph people at prayer, and treat the grounds as somebody's local rather than a backdrop. That is the whole etiquette, and it is what makes the difference between a place that stays quiet and one that doesn't.

title: How to Spend 10 Days in Japan Without a Single Tourist Trap
excerpt: Most first-time visitors follow the same Golden Route — Tokyo, Kyoto, Osaka — and come home feeling like they saw a theme park. This itinerary takes a different approach: slower, deeper, and built around the neighborhoods that locals actually use.
heroImageAlt: A quiet local train platform in Japan at sunrise during a slow travel itinerary
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: The problem with the Golden Route
paragraphs: Tokyo, Kyoto, Osaka in ten days is the default because it works: the Shinkansen connects all three, every hotel speaks some English, and you will see genuinely famous things. The failure mode is subtler than 'too many tourists'. It is that you spend the trip in the thin commercial layer that has grown up around the famous things, and never touch the ordinary country underneath. The fix is not to avoid the big cities. It is to change what you do inside them and to give a couple of days to somewhere that isn't on the list.

sections.heading: Days 1–3: Tokyo, in one or two neighbourhoods
paragraphs: Resist the urge to tick off districts. Pick a base in a residential-but-connected area — Yanaka, Kagurazaka, Koenji or Kiyosumi rather than Shinjuku — and treat it as a home rather than a hotel. Spend a full day walking one area properly: the shopping street, the coin laundry, the standing bar, the shrine at the end of the road. Then use the trains for one or two set pieces you actually care about, not five you feel obliged to see. Three days spent this way leaves a stronger impression than a week of highlights.

sections.heading: Day 4: a day trip instead of a transfer
paragraphs: Before leaving Tokyo, spend one day outside it. Kamakura is the obvious choice and deserves it — coastal, full of temples, walkable. Less obvious options include Chichibu in the mountains north-west, Kawagoe for its surviving merchant streetscape, or Enoshima for a slightly scruffy seaside afternoon. The point is to see what a smaller Japanese town looks like before your sense of the country is set by two metropolises.

sections.heading: Days 5–7: Kyoto, mostly on foot and mostly early
paragraphs: Kyoto punishes late starts more than any other Japanese city. The famous sites are close to empty before eight and unpleasant by eleven, so invert the day: temples at dawn, a long lunch, neighbourhoods and river in the afternoon, dinner somewhere with no English menu. Give one full day to the north — Kurama, Kibune, Ohara — which is where Kyoto stops feeling like a museum. Base yourself away from the station and around Nishijin or Demachiyanagi if you can.

sections.heading: Days 8–9: the deviation that makes the trip
paragraphs: This is the part most itineraries skip. Take two days somewhere that isn't on the Tokyo–Kyoto–Osaka axis. Kanazawa for craft and a genuinely great market. Matsumoto for the castle and the mountains behind it. Naoshima for contemporary art on a small island. Takayama and the Hida valley for old timber townscape. Any of these is reachable in half a day and none of them will feel like the previous week. If you only change one thing about a standard itinerary, change this.

sections.heading: Day 10: Osaka, or don't
paragraphs: Osaka is worth a day for eating and for the fact that it is culturally nothing like Kyoto despite being half an hour away. But it is also fine to skip. If your flight leaves from Kansai, spend the last day there and eat well in Shinsekai or the streets around Tsuruhashi. If it leaves from Tokyo, use the last day to go back to whichever neighbourhood you liked most and do nothing in particular. A repeat visit to one place you already understand is a better ending than a new city you'll see for six hours.

sections.heading: The practical spine
paragraphs: Two things make this shape of trip work. First, fewer hotel changes: three bases over ten days, not six. Packing and checking in eats more of a trip than people expect. Second, a hard limit of two scheduled items per day, with everything else left open. The parts of a Japan trip people describe years later are almost never the scheduled ones — they are the wrong turn, the shop that was still open, the train window between two places you meant to be.

title: The Perfect Route up Mt. Fuji: What Nobody Tells You
excerpt: Climbing Fuji is one of those experiences that sounds straightforward until you're doing it at 3am in a headlamp queue. The mountain rewards preparation and punishes assumptions — here's what we learned from five ascents across different seasons.
heroImageAlt: A rocky Mt. Fuji climbing trail before sunrise with hikers silhouetted in the distance
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: The season is shorter than you think
paragraphs: Fuji has an official climbing season, roughly early July to early September, and it exists for good reasons. Outside it the mountain huts are shut, the first-aid stations are unstaffed, the trails ice over above the treeline, and buses to the trailheads stop running. Climbing outside the season is not a scenic variation; it is genuine alpinism on a volcano with notoriously bad weather. Within the season, the mountain is busy, well-marked, and manageable for anyone reasonably fit. Plan for the season.

sections.heading: Four routes, and why most people take Yoshida
paragraphs: There are four trails to the summit. Yoshida on the north side is the busiest by a wide margin: most huts, most first-aid, separate ascent and descent paths, and the easiest access from Tokyo. Subashiri is quieter and joins Yoshida near the top. Gotemba is the longest and lowest-starting, with a famous scree run on the descent that is either the best or worst part of the trip depending on your knees. Fujinomiya is the shortest and steepest, and the closest to the true summit. A first ascent should almost certainly be Yoshida.

sections.heading: The overnight split is the whole strategy
paragraphs: The single decision that determines how the climb goes is whether you sleep. The common pattern is to start in the afternoon, climb to a hut somewhere around the seventh or eighth station, sleep a few hours, and continue before dawn. The alternative — climbing straight through the night without stopping, sometimes called a bullet climb — is what produces most of the altitude sickness and most of the miserable summit photographs. Book a hut. They are basic, communal and not cheap, but they are the difference between an experience and an ordeal.

sections.heading: Altitude is the actual difficulty
paragraphs: Fuji is not technical. There is no scrambling that requires skill and no exposure that requires nerve. What it has is a summit approaching 3,776 metres and a trailhead that buses drop you at around 2,300, which is a fast gain for a body that woke up at sea level. Headache and nausea above the eighth station are common. The countermeasures are dull and effective: spend an hour at the fifth station before starting, walk slower than feels natural, drink far more water than you want to, and if symptoms get worse rather than better, go down. Descending is the only reliable cure.

sections.heading: What to actually carry
paragraphs: Layers, because the summit can be near freezing while the trailhead is warm, and wind is the real problem rather than temperature. A headlamp, not a phone torch, because you will be walking in the dark and you need your hands. Cash in small coins for the toilets, which are paid and often the only ones for an hour. Two litres of water minimum, or money to buy more at hut prices, which rise with altitude. Gloves, mainly for the rocky sections near the top. Rain gear regardless of the forecast.

sections.heading: Sunrise, and the queue that comes with it
paragraphs: Goraiko — sunrise seen from the summit — is the reason most people climb, and in the peak weeks the final stretch of the Yoshida trail becomes a slow-moving line of headlamps that can add an hour or more. Two ways around it. Watch the sunrise from the eighth station instead, which is nearly as good and far calmer, then continue afterwards. Or climb on a weekday, ideally in early July or the last week of the season, when the volume drops noticeably. The mountain is the same either way.

sections.heading: The descent nobody prepares for
paragraphs: Going down takes about half the time and does most of the damage. The Yoshida descent is a long series of switchbacks in loose volcanic gravel with no shade and very little to look at, and it is where sore knees and blisters actually happen. Trekking poles help more here than on the way up. So do boots that fit properly with enough room at the toe. Budget three to four hours, keep drinking, and be aware that the last bus from the fifth station leaves earlier than you expect.

sections.heading: The old saying about climbing twice
paragraphs: There is a Japanese proverb to the effect that a wise person climbs Fuji once and a fool climbs it twice. It is affectionate rather than dismissive. Fuji is not a beautiful mountain to be on — it is a bare grey cone with a vending machine every few hundred metres — but it is a remarkable mountain to be on top of, and the view of it from the ground afterwards is permanently different. Go once, do it properly, and enjoy looking at it from a train window for the rest of your life.

title: Osaka in 3 Days: The Eating and Wandering Itinerary
excerpt: Osaka has a reputation as Japan's kitchen, but that barely scratches the surface. This city rewards those who eat their way through it without a plan — we've structured the chaos into three days that still feel spontaneous.
heroImageAlt: A lively Osaka evening food street with warm lanterns and small restaurants
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Osaka runs on a different setting
paragraphs: Kyoto is thirty minutes away and might as well be another country. Osaka is louder, blunter and much more interested in feeding you. People talk to strangers. Shop staff joke rather than perform. The local dialect is faster and warmer than Tokyo Japanese, and the city's self-image is built around food and comedy rather than history. Three days is enough to get the shape of it, provided you spend most of them eating and walking rather than travelling between attractions.

sections.heading: Day 1: Namba, Dotonbori and the streets behind them
paragraphs: Start in the middle. Dotonbori — the canal with the running-man sign — is the most photographed strip in the city and worth twenty minutes before you leave it behind. The value is in the streets immediately around it: Hozenji Yokocho, a two-block lane of stone paving and tiny restaurants beside a moss-covered statue that visitors ladle water onto; the covered arcades running north and south; and the Kuromon market for lunch. Eat takoyaki standing up, then again somewhere else, because the difference between a good and bad one is larger than it sounds.

sections.heading: Day 1 evening: Shinsekai
paragraphs: South of Namba, Shinsekai was built as a vision of the future in 1912 and has been comfortably decaying ever since. The Tsutenkaku tower sits at the centre of a grid of kushikatsu restaurants — skewered, breaded, deep-fried everything — where the one rule is that you do not double-dip in the communal sauce. It is slightly seedy, entirely safe, and the closest thing in Japan to a city centre that hasn't been tidied up. Go hungry.

sections.heading: Day 2: Kita, coffee and the department store basements
paragraphs: Spend the morning around Umeda in the north. This is the business half of the city and it is where the food gets serious: the basement floors of the big department stores hold some of the best prepared food in Japan, and lunch sets in the restaurant floors above are heavily subsidised versions of dinner. Nakazakicho, a few minutes east, is a pocket of prewar houses converted into coffee shops and secondhand stores that survived redevelopment more or less by accident. It is the best walking in the city.

sections.heading: Day 2 evening: Tenma and the longest arcade
paragraphs: Tenjinbashisuji is the longest shopping arcade in Japan, running for around two and a half kilometres, and the section around Tenma station turns into a dense grid of standing bars in the evening. This is where Osaka eats when it isn't performing for anyone. Order by pointing, expect to share a counter, and accept that you will end up talking to whoever is next to you. Budget less than you think — the point of the format is volume and cheapness.

sections.heading: Day 3: one castle, one deviation
paragraphs: Osaka Castle is a concrete reconstruction with a lift inside, which disappoints people who wanted the original. Go anyway, but go for the park: the outer moat and stonework are genuinely enormous, and the grounds are where the city relaxes. Then take the afternoon somewhere off the tourist map. Tsuruhashi, around the station, is the centre of Osaka's Korean community and has the best grilled meat in the city. Shinsaibashi's back streets have the secondhand clothing. Either is a better final afternoon than a second castle.

sections.heading: How to eat here without a plan
paragraphs: The Osaka approach is kuidaore — roughly, eating yourself into ruin — and it is best served by ordering less at each stop and making more stops. Three small things at three places beats one large meal. Look for queues of locals rather than English menus, sit at counters rather than tables, and if a place has one item on the sign, order that item. Cash is still useful in the older arcades. Almost nothing here needs a reservation, which is precisely why the city is easy to travel in.

title: Yakushima: Japan's Ancient Forest That Few Tourists Find
excerpt: A UNESCO-listed island covered in cedar trees that are older than many civilizations, Yakushima sits off the southern tip of Kyushu and sees a fraction of the visitors it deserves. The hike through Shiratani Unsuikyo inspired Princess Mononoke — and it still feels that way.
heroImageAlt: A misty ancient cedar forest path in Yakushima covered with moss
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: An island that makes its own weather
paragraphs: Yakushima sits off the southern tip of Kyushu, is roughly circular, and rises to nearly two thousand metres almost immediately from the sea. That geometry produces one of the wettest climates in Japan — there is a local saying about it raining thirty-five days a month — and the rain is the entire point. It is why the island is covered in moss, why the cedars grow the way they do, and why the forest looks like something rendered rather than grown. Expect to be wet. Plan around it rather than against it.

sections.heading: Getting there, which is most of the filter
paragraphs: Access is by ferry or short flight from Kagoshima, and that single transfer is why the island stays quiet. The fast ferry takes a couple of hours, the slower car ferry longer, and flights are small and weather-dependent. Once on the island there is a coastal road, an infrequent bus service, and not much else — most visitors rent a car, and it is the right call. Nothing about Yakushima works well as a day trip. Give it three nights minimum.

sections.heading: Shiratani Unsuikyo, and the Mononoke question
paragraphs: Shiratani Unsuikyo is the accessible one: a network of trails through granite boulders, clear streams and cedar forest, with routes from about an hour to a full day. The upper section, sometimes called the Mononoke forest, is widely described as the inspiration for the landscape in Princess Mononoke — the connection is real in the sense that the film's art team visited, though the film itself is not set here. It doesn't matter. The moss genuinely does cover everything, the light genuinely is green, and photographs consistently fail to convey it.

sections.heading: Jomon Sugi is a full day and a commitment
paragraphs: The island's most famous tree is a yakusugi cedar estimated at anywhere from two to seven thousand years old, depending on which dating method you trust. Reaching it is a long day — commonly around ten hours round trip, much of it walking a disused logging railway line in the dark at the start. There is a bus system to the trailhead that replaces private access during the busy season, and it starts very early. It is a genuine hike rather than a walk, and it is not the best forest on the island. Do it if the tree matters to you; skip it without guilt if it doesn't.

sections.heading: The rest of the island
paragraphs: Yakushima is not only forest. There are hot springs on the shore at Hirauchi that are only accessible at low tide and have no walls. There are sea turtles nesting on the western beaches in early summer. The western coastal road runs through untouched forest where deer and macaques sit in the road and regard your car with contempt. Ohko-no-taki and Senpiro-no-taki are both roadside waterfalls of a scale that would be a national park centrepiece anywhere else.

sections.heading: What to bring, given the rain
paragraphs: Proper waterproofs rather than a folding umbrella, because the trails are steep and you will need both hands. Boots with grip — wet granite and wet cedar roots are the main hazard on the island and account for most injuries. A dry bag for a camera and phone. More socks than seems reasonable. Cash, because the island's shops and guesthouses are not uniformly card-friendly. Almost none of this is exotic; it is just that people arrive with city clothing and regret it within an hour.

sections.heading: Why it stays empty
paragraphs: Yakushima is a UNESCO World Heritage site, an hour from a major airport, and objectively one of the most extraordinary landscapes in the country — and it receives a small fraction of the visitors that a comparable place in Honshu would. The reasons are mundane: the transfer, the weather, and the fact that it requires a car and a few days rather than a bullet-train afternoon. Those same reasons are why the forest is still quiet. It is the rare case where the inconvenience is doing something useful.

title: How to Read a Japanese Menu Without Speaking Japanese
excerpt: Most Japanese restaurants don't have English menus, and that's not a problem once you know what to look for. A handful of kanji, some pattern recognition, and the willingness to point gets you through almost any restaurant in the country.
heroImageAlt: A Japanese restaurant menu on a table with chopsticks and a bowl of noodles nearby
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: The three kinds of menu you will meet
paragraphs: Japanese restaurant menus fall into roughly three types, and knowing which one you are looking at solves most of the problem. There is the photographic menu, common in chains and family restaurants, where you can simply point. There is the laminated or printed menu in Japanese only, usually at specialist shops that do one thing. And there is the handwritten wall menu, which changes daily and is the hardest to read but almost always signals a place worth eating at. The wall menu is a good sign, not a warning.

sections.heading: Twenty or so characters carry most of the meaning
paragraphs: You do not need to read Japanese. You need to recognise a small set of repeated characters. The proteins: 肉 meat, 牛 beef, 豚 pork, 鶏 chicken, 魚 fish, 海老 shrimp, 卵 egg. The staples: 米 and ご飯 rice, 麺 noodles, 蕎麦 soba, 饂飩 or うどん udon, パン bread. The methods: 焼 grilled, 揚 fried, 煮 simmered, 蒸 steamed, 生 raw. Learn to spot those thirty-odd shapes and a menu stops being opaque and becomes a puzzle with most of the pieces filled in.

sections.heading: Set meals are the shortcut
paragraphs: Look for 定食 (teishoku) and セット (setto). A teishoku is a set meal — a main dish with rice, miso soup and pickles — and it is almost always the best value on the menu and the most complete meal. At lunch, ランチ (ranchi) usually indicates a discounted midday version of the same food served at dinner. If you can find nothing else on a menu, finding the teishoku section is enough to order well.

sections.heading: The ticket machine, which is easier than it looks
paragraphs: Many ramen, curry and gyudon shops have a vending machine by the door. You pay first, it prints a ticket, you hand the ticket to the counter. The convention is that the top-left button is the shop's flagship dish — the thing they want you to order and the thing they are best at. If you are unsure, press the top-left button. Machines increasingly have English toggles, and most have photographs. The awkwardness is entirely in the first ten seconds.

sections.heading: Plastic food, and why it is genuinely useful
paragraphs: The replica food in restaurant windows is not a tourist gimmick; it predates mass tourism and exists because it works. It is an accurate guide to portion size and composition, which photographs often are not. If a display case shows what you want, it is completely normal to walk in, and if there is any confusion, walking out and pointing at the case is an established move rather than an embarrassment.

sections.heading: Six phrases that cover almost everything
paragraphs: Sumimasen — excuse me, and the way you get attention. Kore o kudasai — this one, please, while pointing. Osusume wa nan desu ka — what do you recommend. Onaji mono o — the same thing again. O-kaikei onegaishimasu — the bill, please. Gochisosama deshita — thank you for the meal, said on the way out. That is a complete restaurant vocabulary. Pronunciation matters less than you fear, because Japanese vowels are consistent and forgiving.

sections.heading: Allergies and restrictions need more than pointing
paragraphs: This is the one place where improvisation is a bad idea. Dashi — stock made from bonito — is in a very large proportion of savoury food including things that look vegetarian, and 'no meat' does not communicate that. If you have a genuine allergy or a strict restriction, carry a written card in Japanese explaining it precisely. Small specialist restaurants often cannot modify dishes, and a clear written note lets them tell you honestly rather than guess.

title: What Wabi-Sabi Really Means — And Why the World Needs It Now
excerpt: The Japanese aesthetic of imperfection and transience offers something Western design philosophy rarely does: permission to be incomplete. Wabi-sabi isn't a style — it's a way of perceiving, and learning to see it changes how you look at almost everything.
heroImageAlt: A weathered ceramic vase in a quiet Japanese room with soft garden light
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Two words doing different jobs
paragraphs: Wabi and sabi were separate ideas long before they were welded into a single phrase. Wabi originally carried a sense of desolation and rustic poverty that gradually turned into something closer to austere simplicity — the beauty of having little and arranging it well. Sabi described what time does to things: patina, weathering, the particular quality of an object that has clearly been used. Roughly, wabi is about the arrangement and sabi is about the ageing. Together they describe an aesthetic that finds sufficiency in the plain and the worn.

sections.heading: It came out of the tea room
paragraphs: The idea was formalised through tea. In the sixteenth century the tea master Sen no Rikyu moved the ceremony away from imported Chinese luxury towards deliberately humble materials: unglazed local ceramics, bamboo, rough plaster walls, an entrance so low that everyone had to stoop to enter. The point was not poverty as a style. It was the removal of anything that distracted from attention. Almost everything now labelled wabi-sabi descends from that editorial decision.

sections.heading: Imperfection, but not carelessness
paragraphs: The common English summary — the beauty of imperfection — is close enough to be useful and loose enough to mislead. Wabi-sabi does not celebrate things being badly made. A wabi tea bowl is the work of a skilled potter who allowed the material and the fire to leave evidence of themselves. The asymmetry is permitted rather than manufactured. The distinction matters because it is the difference between an object that shows its making and an object that is distressed on purpose to look old.

sections.heading: Impermanence is the load-bearing part
paragraphs: Underneath the aesthetics is a Buddhist observation that nothing lasts, including you. This is why the cherry blossom is the national flower rather than something more durable: it is admired specifically because it falls within a week. Mono no aware, a related idea, names the particular sadness of being aware that a moment is passing while you are still inside it. Wabi-sabi is what that awareness looks like when applied to objects and rooms rather than to feelings.

sections.heading: Where to actually see it
paragraphs: It is easier to recognise than to define. A Raku tea bowl in a museum, hand-formed rather than thrown, thick-walled and irregular. A temple garden in Kyoto where the moss has been allowed to take the stones. An old wooden building where the timber has silvered and the floor has worn into a slight bowl at the threshold. A shop counter polished by sixty years of forearms. None of these were designed to be photogenic, which is a substantial part of why they are.

sections.heading: Why it travels badly
paragraphs: Exported, wabi-sabi tends to become a shopping category: expensive rough ceramics, muted colours, linen. That is a style, and styles are fine, but it inverts the original idea, which was about spending less attention on objects rather than more money on the right ones. The useful version is not a palette. It is the habit of noticing that the chipped mug you have used every morning for nine years is more interesting than a new one, and declining to replace it.

sections.heading: What it offers now
paragraphs: The reason the idea keeps being rediscovered outside Japan is that it argues against two things modern life is heavily invested in: the pursuit of the flawless and the assumption that new is better. Wabi-sabi proposes that wear is information, that incompleteness leaves room for attention, and that things reaching their end are not thereby diminished. You do not need to redecorate to take that on. It is mostly a change in what you are willing to find sufficient.

title: Kintsugi: The Art of Repairing Broken Things with Gold
excerpt: A 500-year-old technique for mending ceramics with lacquer mixed with gold, silver, or platinum has become a global metaphor for resilience. We visited a master craftsman in Kyoto to understand why kintsugi is about far more than broken bowls.
heroImageAlt: A repaired ceramic kintsugi bowl with gold seams on an artisan worktable
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: What it actually is
paragraphs: Kintsugi — golden joinery — repairs broken ceramics with urushi lacquer, then dusts the seams with powdered gold, silver or platinum. The result is a bowl whose fracture lines are the most conspicuous thing about it. The technique is usually dated to the fifteenth or sixteenth century, and the frequently repeated origin story involves a shogun sending a damaged tea bowl to China for repair and being dissatisfied with the metal staples that came back. Whether or not that particular account is reliable, the practice grew up alongside the tea ceremony and its taste for objects with history.

sections.heading: Lacquer is the real material
paragraphs: The gold gets the attention; the lacquer does the work. Urushi is sap from the lacquer tree, and it is both the adhesive and the structure of the repair. It cures through humidity rather than drying, so pieces spend days or weeks in a damp cabinet between stages, and each layer must harden before the next goes on. Raw urushi is also a skin irritant closely related to poison ivy, which is one reason the craft has always been specialist work. A genuine repair takes weeks to months, not an afternoon.

sections.heading: Three recognised styles
paragraphs: Practitioners distinguish between roughly three approaches. Crack kintsugi joins clean breaks with a thin gold seam. Piece-method kintsugi replaces a missing fragment with a solid area of lacquer and gold. Joint-call kintsugi — the most striking — fills a gap with a shard from a completely different vessel, so the finished bowl visibly contains two histories. The last of these makes the philosophy hardest to ignore: the repair is not attempting to return the object to a previous state at all.

sections.heading: Where to see it and where to try it
paragraphs: Kyoto is the centre for both. Museum collections hold repaired tea ware, and a number of workshops in the city and in Tokyo run short courses for visitors — typically half a day, usually using a synthetic substitute for urushi to avoid the curing time and the skin reaction. That substitution is worth understanding before you book: a two-hour class produces something real and satisfying, but it is a demonstration of the aesthetic rather than the traditional technique. Ask which material a workshop uses if it matters to you.

sections.heading: Buying repaired pieces
paragraphs: Antique shops and flea markets — Toji temple market in Kyoto, Oedo in Tokyo — turn up kintsugi pieces regularly, at prices ranging from modest to serious. Two things to check. Real gold seams are matte and slightly uneven under the light rather than uniformly bright, and genuine urushi repairs have a slight softness at the edge of the seam. Also ask whether a piece is food-safe; older repairs and some modern synthetic ones are not, and a bowl for display is a different purchase from a bowl for tea.

sections.heading: The metaphor, and its limits
paragraphs: Kintsugi has become globally popular as a metaphor for resilience: the break is part of the object, the repair is not concealed, the thing is more valuable for having been damaged. That reading is not a Western invention — it is close to what the tea masters were getting at. It is worth adding the part that usually falls off in translation: kintsugi is slow, expensive, requires a specialist, and cannot be done to every break. The metaphor is more honest when it keeps the labour in.

title: Hanami 2026: Where to See Cherry Blossoms Like a Local
excerpt: Skip the tourist crowds at Maruyama Park and Ueno. The best hanami spots are the ones you stumble into — a neighborhood embankment, a school gate, a canal nobody bothered to list. We've found them, so you don't have to.
heroImageAlt: A peaceful riverside hanami picnic scene under cherry blossoms in Japan
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: The forecast is a national institution
paragraphs: Cherry blossom timing is tracked and published every spring in considerable detail, with a front that moves roughly northwards from Kyushu in late March to Hokkaido in early May. Tokyo and Kyoto typically open somewhere in the last week of March and reach full bloom — mankai — around a week later. The useful thing to understand is the shape rather than the dates: from first flowers to peak is about a week, peak lasts a few days, and a single day of rain or wind can end it. Check the forecast in the fortnight before you travel, and hold your plans loosely.

sections.heading: Full bloom is not the best part
paragraphs: Two underrated windows sit either side of mankai. The days just before, when the trees are perhaps seventy per cent open, are quieter and the colour is stronger. And the days just after, when the petals come down — hanafubuki, a blossom blizzard — are the ones people actually remember. If your dates are fixed and you miss the peak by a few days in either direction, you have not missed the thing. You have probably got a better version of it with fewer people.

sections.heading: Why the famous parks disappoint
paragraphs: Ueno and Maruyama are genuinely spectacular and genuinely unbearable. They operate less like parks than like festivals: tarpaulins claimed from early morning, food stalls, crowds moving at a shuffle, and in the case of Ueno, a designated route. If that atmosphere is what you want, go, and go early. If what you pictured was standing under a tree, they will be a disappointment, and the alternative is not far away.

sections.heading: Look for water, schools and railways
paragraphs: The reliable rule is that cherry trees in Japan were planted along three kinds of edge: rivers and canals, school and public-building grounds, and old railway embankments. Any residential neighbourhood with a canal running through it will have a line of trees over the water and almost nobody looking at them. In Tokyo, the smaller waterways in the east and the residential stretches of the Kanda and Meguro rivers away from their famous sections. In Kyoto, the canal paths north of the Philosopher's Path and the Kamo river banks well upstream of the centre. None of these need naming precisely — the pattern is the point.

sections.heading: Yozakura, the evening version
paragraphs: Many locations light the trees after dark, and blossom under artificial light against a black sky is a completely different object from blossom against a blue one. Castle grounds and temple gardens often run limited evening openings during the bloom, usually ticketed and usually only for a week or two. It is also the version with the fewest daytime crowds. Bring a layer; late March evenings in Kyoto are colder than the afternoon suggests.

sections.heading: How to actually do hanami
paragraphs: The practice is simple and social: a sheet on the ground, food from a convenience store or department store basement, something to drink, and several hours of sitting under a tree talking. Shoes come off at the edge of the sheet. Take everything away with you, including the bag — bins are scarce and the expectation is total. Some parks prohibit alcohol and some prohibit sheets entirely, and signs will say so. Beyond that there is no ceremony to get right. Sitting down is the whole activity.

title: The Best Japanese Kitchen Knives to Bring Home
excerpt: Japanese knives are the single best souvenir you can carry out of Japan — functional, beautiful, and something you'll use every day for decades. This guide covers every price point from a ¥4,000 entry knife to the hand-forged blade worth saving up for.
heroImageAlt: Japanese kitchen knives displayed on a dark wooden shop counter
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Why the knives are different
paragraphs: The short version is geometry and steel. A typical Western chef's knife is ground with a symmetrical edge at a relatively wide angle and made from softer stainless steel that bends before it chips. A traditional Japanese knife is often ground on one side only, at a much narrower angle, from harder steel that holds an edge far longer and is correspondingly more brittle. The result cuts better and tolerates less abuse. That trade is the whole decision, and it is worth understanding before you spend anything.

sections.heading: The three shapes worth considering
paragraphs: Ignore the long catalogue and start with three. The santoku is the general-purpose home knife — shortish, flat-bellied, good at almost everything, and the safest single purchase. The gyuto is the Japanese take on a Western chef's knife, longer with more curve, better if you already cook with a chef's knife and want the same motion. The nakiri is a rectangular vegetable knife that looks alarming and is superb at exactly one job. If you buy one knife, buy a santoku or a gyuto. If you buy two, add the nakiri.

sections.heading: Steel, and the honest trade-off
paragraphs: Carbon steel — shirogami and aogami, white and blue paper steel — takes the sharpest edge and is what most traditional makers prefer. It also rusts if you leave it wet for ten minutes and will discolour within weeks. Stainless resists all of that and gives up a little sharpness and a little edge retention. Clad or san-mai construction splits the difference: a hard carbon core for the edge with stainless sides for protection. For most people buying a knife on holiday, clad stainless is the right answer, and admitting that is not a compromise.

sections.heading: What each price bracket actually buys
paragraphs: Around ¥4,000–8,000 gets a competent machine-made stainless santoku from an established brand, which will outperform most knives in a Western home kitchen. Around ¥10,000–20,000 is the broad sweet spot: better steel, better fit and finish, often a clad blade and a proper wooden handle. Above roughly ¥30,000 you are paying for hand-forging, a named smith and single-bevel geometry, which rewards skill and punishes its absence. Prices move, so treat these as brackets rather than quotes.

sections.heading: Where to buy in Tokyo and elsewhere
paragraphs: Kappabashi in Tokyo is the restaurant-supply district and the obvious destination — several streets of knife shops, many with English-speaking staff, ranging from workaday to serious. Sakai in Osaka and Seki in Gifu are the traditional forging towns and worth a detour if the knives are the reason for the trip. Department store kitchenware floors carry good mid-range stock with reliable service. Avoid airport gift shops and souvenir stalls near tourist sites, where the markup is high and the provenance vague.

sections.heading: Buying well in the shop
paragraphs: Hold it. The single most useful test is whether the handle sits comfortably in your grip, and it is the one thing no online description conveys. Ask whether the blade is single or double bevel, and if single, whether it is ground for a right- or left-handed user — a left-handed cook with a right-ground single bevel will have a bad time. Ask what steel it is. A good shop will answer all three immediately, will offer to sharpen it before you leave, and will often engrave it. A shop that cannot answer is telling you something.

sections.heading: Getting it home legally
paragraphs: Never in hand luggage. It will be confiscated at security, and this happens constantly. Pack it in checked baggage, in the box, ideally with the blade guard the shop provides and the whole thing wrapped and taped. Keep the receipt accessible. Most countries permit kitchen knives in checked luggage without issue, but a small number regulate blade length or type on arrival, so check your own country's rules before you buy something expensive. If you are shipping instead, most reputable shops will arrange it.

sections.heading: Keeping it once you have it
paragraphs: Hand wash, dry immediately, and never put it in a dishwasher — the detergent and the heat will ruin both the edge and a wooden handle. Cut on wood or plastic, never glass, stone or a ceramic plate. Do not use it to cut through bone or frozen food; the thin hard edge will chip. And learn to use a whetstone, which is less difficult than it sounds and is the only way to maintain the edge properly, since pull-through sharpeners are designed for wider Western angles and will grind the geometry away.

title: Buying Matcha: Ceremonial vs. Culinary Grade Explained
excerpt: The matcha market is flooded with products that taste nothing like what you drink in a tea ceremony — and the price tag is not a reliable guide. Here's how to read labels, what to taste for, and where to buy the real thing.
heroImageAlt: Matcha powder in ceramic bowls with a bamboo whisk and tea scoop
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: What matcha actually is
paragraphs: Matcha is powdered green tea from leaves that were shaded for several weeks before harvest. The shading starves the plant of light, which raises the amino acid content — particularly theanine — and lowers bitterness, producing the sweetness and savoury depth that distinguishes good matcha. The leaves are then steamed, dried, destemmed and deveined into a form called tencha, and stone-ground into powder. That grinding is slow, and it is a large part of why the good stuff costs what it does.

sections.heading: Ceremonial and culinary are marketing terms
paragraphs: Neither phrase is a regulated grade. There is no certifying body and no legal definition, and a tin labelled ceremonial can be almost anything. What the words usually gesture at is real, though: 'ceremonial' generally means an earlier harvest intended to be whisked with water and drunk alone, and 'culinary' generally means a later harvest with more bitterness, meant to survive being mixed with milk and sugar. Treat the label as a hint about intended use rather than a statement of quality.

sections.heading: What to look for instead
paragraphs: Four things carry more information than the grade name. Colour: vivid, almost fluorescent green means shaded leaf and careful handling; dull, yellowish or olive powder means age, oxidation or lower-grade leaf. Origin: Uji in Kyoto, Nishio in Aichi, and Yame in Fukuoka are the established regions and reputable producers say so on the tin. Harvest or milling date, because matcha degrades quickly once ground. And packaging: opaque, airtight and small. A large clear jar is a bad sign regardless of price.

sections.heading: Price is a weak signal on its own
paragraphs: Cost tells you something but not enough. Very cheap matcha — the sort sold in large pouches at a suspiciously low price per gram — is almost always late-harvest and will taste flatly bitter no matter how you prepare it. But expensive matcha in an ornate presentation box is frequently priced for gift-giving rather than for what is inside. The most reliable purchases sit in the middle: a modest 20 to 40 gram tin from a named producer, bought somewhere with turnover.

sections.heading: Where to buy
paragraphs: Established tea houses are the best option and many will let you taste before buying, which settles the question faster than any label. In Kyoto, the shops around Uji are the obvious destination and worth the short train ride. Department store basement food halls carry good producers with reliable stock rotation. Specialist tea shops in any major city are generally trustworthy. Souvenir shops at stations and airports are where old stock goes to be sold in decorative boxes, and the difference in the cup is immediately obvious.

sections.heading: Making it well enough to tell the difference
paragraphs: You need a bowl, a bamboo whisk and ideally a small sieve. Sift about two grams to break the clumps, which is the step everyone skips and the one that causes most bad results. Add roughly 60 to 70 millilitres of water at around 80°C — not boiling, which scalds the powder and makes it harsh. Whisk briskly in a W motion until a fine even foam forms. Good matcha at this point is sweet and thick with a savoury finish. If it is simply bitter, the problem is usually the water temperature or the tea, in that order.

sections.heading: Getting it home and keeping it
paragraphs: Matcha's enemies are air, light, heat and moisture, and it declines noticeably within a few weeks of opening. Buy small quantities rather than one large tin, keep it sealed, and store it in the refrigerator once opened — letting the tin come back to room temperature before opening, so condensation does not form inside. Unopened tins travel fine in either checked or hand luggage. If you are bringing back gifts, buy them last and keep them out of a hot car.

title: 10 Japanese Drugstore Products Worth Every Yen
excerpt: Japanese pharmacies are overwhelming in the best way — walls of skincare, hair treatments, and stomach remedies at prices that make no sense until you try them. These are the ten products that actually earn their place in your luggage.
heroImageAlt: Japanese drugstore skincare and travel products arranged neatly on bright shelves
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Why the drugstores are like this
paragraphs: Japanese pharmacy chains — Matsumoto Kiyoshi, Sundrug, Welcia and the rest — occupy a strange middle ground between a chemist and a small department store, and the skincare aisle in particular operates at a standard that is elsewhere reserved for premium brands. The reason is competitive: domestic consumers are unusually informed about ingredients and formulation, and the mass-market brands compete on substance rather than packaging. The practical consequence for a visitor is that the ¥800 product is frequently very good.

sections.heading: Sunscreen, which is the strongest category
paragraphs: If you buy one thing, buy sunscreen. Japanese formulations are widely regarded as the best mass-market sun protection available, largely because the regulatory environment permits UV filters that are elegant, stable and pleasant to wear — which is what actually determines whether people reapply. Expect fluid, weightless textures that sit under makeup without pilling. Look for PA++++ alongside the SPF number, which indicates UVA protection. The well-known gel and milk formats from the major cosmetics houses cost a fraction of what comparable products cost abroad.

sections.heading: Sheet masks and the hydration aisle
paragraphs: Sheet masks are sold in packs of thirty or more at a price that makes the boutique single-mask model look absurd. The large-volume packs from the mainstream brands are the ones locals buy in quantity — unfragranced, simple humectant formulas, meant to be used daily rather than as a treat. Also in this aisle: hatomugi and similar large-bottle lotions, sold in half-litre containers designed to be used generously on face and body. Neither category is glamorous and both are the reason people's luggage comes back heavier.

sections.heading: Cleansing oils and balms
paragraphs: Double cleansing — an oil to remove sunscreen and makeup, then a foaming wash — is standard practice in Japan, and the cleansing oil category reflects decades of refinement. The mass-market oils emulsify cleanly, rinse without residue, and cost very little for a large pump bottle. If you have only used a wipe or a micellar water, this is the single change most likely to be noticeable. Buy the large size; it is heavy but the price per use is the point.

sections.heading: Steam eye masks and the comfort aisle
paragraphs: Self-heating eye masks that warm gently for around ten minutes are a genuinely Japanese invention and difficult to find abroad at a sensible price. They come in boxes, in several scents, and they are the most reliably appreciated small gift on this list. Nearby you will find heat patches for shoulders and lower back, cooling sheets for fever and hot days, and a large selection of foot-care products aimed at people who walk a great deal, which after a week in Japan will include you.

sections.heading: The medicine cabinet items
paragraphs: Beyond cosmetics, a few pharmacy staples are worth knowing about. There are well-established stomach remedies formulated for overeating, sold in sachets and widely used. There are effective liquid bandage products. There are eye drops in a range of formulations that is bewildering by international standards. These are actual medicines: read the packaging, ask the pharmacist, and be aware that some products behind the counter require a brief conversation. If you take prescription medication, check the import rules before you travel, as Japan restricts several compounds that are unremarkable elsewhere.

sections.heading: Tax-free, and how to actually get it
paragraphs: Most large drugstores offer tax-free purchasing above a minimum spend for visitors, and consumables and general goods are counted in separate categories. Bring your physical passport — a photograph is not accepted. Consumable items are sealed in a bag that you are not supposed to open before leaving the country, so buy the things you want to use during the trip separately. The saving is meaningful on a large basket, and the queue at the tax-free counter is usually shorter in the early afternoon.

sections.heading: A note on how to choose
paragraphs: The aisle is overwhelming because almost everything in it is competent, which is a better problem than the alternative. Two shortcuts: the products with the plainest packaging and the largest volume are generally what locals restock rather than what is marketed to visitors, and staff will point you at the right shelf if you show them the back of your hand or say the category name. Buying three products you will actually finish beats buying twelve that look interesting in a photograph.

title: Where to Buy Authentic Yukata in Tokyo Without the Markup
excerpt: The tourist-district yukata sold near Asakusa are fine, but the ones sold at department store basements and specialist shops are extraordinary — and often cheaper. This guide takes you past the obvious options to the places worth visiting.
heroImageAlt: Folded cotton yukata fabrics and obi sashes displayed in a Tokyo shop
author: TABI Editorial

sections.heading: Yukata is not kimono
paragraphs: A yukata is unlined cotton, worn in summer, at festivals, at fireworks displays and around hot-spring towns, and it is the informal end of Japanese dress. A kimono is lined, usually silk, formal, structurally more complex and considerably more expensive. Conflating the two is the most common mistake visitors make, and it matters commercially: a shop quoting a very low price for a 'kimono' is almost certainly selling a yukata, and a shop quoting a very high price for a yukata is relying on you not knowing the difference.

sections.heading: What you actually need to buy
paragraphs: A wearable yukata is at minimum three items: the yukata itself, an obi sash, and something to hold the whole thing closed underneath — a koshihimo tie, and ideally a datejime belt. Many shops sell these as a set, which is the sensible way to buy your first one. Add geta sandals and a kinchaku drawstring bag if you want the complete look, though neither is essential. A yukata bought alone, with no obi, is a garment you will not be able to wear.

sections.heading: The Asakusa question
paragraphs: The shops clustered around Asakusa and Nakamise are convenient and not a scam. What they are is optimised for a specific transaction: a tourist buying one yukata, quickly, in a place with high rent. The quality is generally acceptable, the printing is often digital rather than dyed, the sizes skew towards the middle, and the price reflects the location. If you want a yukata this afternoon and are not going to think about it again, this is a perfectly reasonable place to buy one. If you have another day, you can do considerably better.

sections.heading: Department store basements and upper floors
paragraphs: The major department stores — the ones with a kimono floor rather than a kimono corner — carry proper stock, often with a summer yukata section from late spring onwards. The advantages are real: consistent sizing including longer lengths, staff who will fit you properly and show you how to tie the obi, dyed rather than printed fabric at the middle price points, and the ability to buy the components separately. Prices start higher than Asakusa and the value is better. Ask for the yukata section by name and be prepared to spend half an hour.

sections.heading: The specialist and secondhand end
paragraphs: Two other options are worth the effort. Specialist kimono shops, found in the older commercial districts rather than the tourist ones, sell to people who wear these clothes regularly and will happily explain the difference between a printed and a hand-dyed pattern. And secondhand — flea markets such as Oedo, and the dedicated recycled-kimono shops — is where the genuinely interesting fabric is, frequently at a fraction of new prices. Secondhand requires you to check for stains at the collar and cuffs and to accept that sizing is whatever it is.

sections.heading: Fit, which is mostly about length
paragraphs: Yukata are not tailored to the body in the Western sense; the excess length is folded and held at the waist. What matters is that the garment is long enough — roughly your own height is the standard guide — and that the sleeves fall where you want them. Visitors taller than about 175 centimetres should specify a long size explicitly, since standard stock often will not work and a too-short yukata is immediately obvious. Shoulder width matters second. Everything else is adjusted by the tying.

sections.heading: Wearing it without getting the important part wrong
paragraphs: Left side over right. Always. The reverse is how the dead are dressed, and it is the one error that Japanese people will notice instantly and find genuinely uncomfortable. Beyond that: the obi sits at the natural waist for men and slightly higher for women, the collar should sit a little away from the back of the neck rather than tight against it, and small steps are simply how the garment moves. Wearing a yukata as a visitor is welcomed rather than resented, provided the left-over-right rule is observed.
